name: Slavic Breaks
description:
Slavic Village broke first. Before the corridor, before the corponations, before Meridian 88 existed as a concept, this neighborhood was already a case study in what happens when capital abandons a place and doesn't come back. The 2108 foreclosure crisis hit Slavic Village harder than almost anywhere else in America — block after block of boarded-up houses, stripped copper, and families who discovered that the American Dream had an expiration date printed in the fine print of their subprime mortgages. A century later, the scars haven't healed. They've been built over, but scars built over are not the same as scars healed.

The Eastern European immigrant legacy that gave the neighborhood its name survives in fragments. The Polish and Czech social clubs are still standing — their reinforced basements serve as community shelters and black-market trading posts. Saint Stanislaus Church, built in 1886, has been converted into a combined medical clinic and augmentation facility operated by a collective of unlicensed practitioners who serve the excluded and Tier 1 populations that corporate healthcare won't touch. The old commercial strips along Fleet Avenue and Broadway have been colonized by salvage operations, repair shops, and the kind of small-scale manufacturing that exists because it's too low-margin for any corponation to bother claiming jurisdiction over.

Slavic Breaks is what the corridor looks like when no one is looking. No corponation has claimed sovereignty here because the economics don't justify the cost of enforcement. Tollgate maintains the water and power infrastructure because it's connected to systems that serve more profitable neighborhoods, but the maintenance is minimal and the outages are frequent. The population is predominantly Tier 1 and excluded — climate refugees, displaced workers, families who have been here for generations and have nowhere else to go. What they have built in the absence of corporate governance is not pretty, but it functions. Mutual aid networks distribute food and medical supplies. The social clubs serve as dispute resolution centers. The old foreclosure houses have been rebuilt by hand, using salvaged materials and Gravemoss biofoam that falls off the supply trucks with suspicious regularity. Slavic Breaks doesn't need the corponations. It has needed them before, and it remembers what happened.

sights: Rows of rebuilt foreclosure houses — original frames wrapped in salvaged materials, Gravemoss biofoam patching the gaps like organic scar tissue
Saint Stanislaus Church, its 1886 stonework intact, a red cross painted on the door marking it as an unlicensed medical facility
Polish and Czech social club signs, faded but maintained, their basements lit by generator power when the grid fails
Salvage yards stretching for blocks, organized with a precision that suggests this economy is not as informal as it appears
Children playing in streets that have no surveillance drones, no corporate signage, no jurisdiction markers — just pavement and people
sounds: Generator hum during the frequent power outages — a sound the neighborhood has learned to sleep through
The clang and grind of salvage operations — metal being sorted, components being tested, value being extracted from waste
Polish and Czech spoken alongside Shelf Cant and Standard — the old languages persist here
Church bells from Saint Stanislaus — rung manually, on a schedule that has nothing to do with the liturgical calendar and everything to do with neighborhood alerts
Quiet — Slavic Breaks is quieter than any corporate zone because there are no drones, no advertisements, no algorithmic soundscapes
smells: Biofoam curing — the sharp chemical tang of Gravemoss material setting into structural form
Wood smoke from heating systems that predate the corridor's power grid
Pierogi and kielbasa from the social club kitchens — recipes that survived the Atlantic crossing and the collapse of the country they crossed to
atmosphere.feel: Slavic Breaks feels like a place that has been punched in the face so many times it has stopped flinching. There is no optimism here, but there is no despair either — just a pragmatic determination to keep functioning that transcends any economic system imposed from outside. The neighborhood doesn't resist the corponations. It has simply outlasted every institution that has ever claimed authority over it.

demographics: Approximately 18,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 and excluded. Significant populations of Eastern European descent families (fourth and fifth generation), Gulf Coast climate refugees, and displaced industrial workers. One of the highest concentrations of unaugmented adults in the Cleveland sprawl — not by choice, but by economics.
economy: Salvage, repair, and small-scale manufacturing. The social clubs operate as informal banks, lending in scrip and barter credits. Medical services through Saint Stanislaus generate a small revenue stream from patients across the city's lower tiers. Gravemoss biofoam, officially 'lost in transit,' is the neighborhood's primary construction material and an informal currency.
power_structure: No corporate sovereignty. Tollgate maintains minimum infrastructure. Governance operates through the social clubs — the Polish American Club, the Czech Heritage Society, and the Fleet Avenue Mutual Aid Collective — which function as a distributed council. Disputes are resolved internally. External threats are met collectively. The system is imperfect and sometimes brutal, but it has kept the neighborhood alive for a century without corporate assistance.
dangers: Infrastructure failure — power outages, water contamination, and structural collapse are regular occurrences
Medical risk — Saint Stanislaus provides essential healthcare but the practitioners are unlicensed and equipment is salvaged
Isolation — Slavic Breaks' lack of corporate jurisdiction means no emergency services, no legal protections, no safety net beyond the community itself
Exploitation — the absence of surveillance makes the neighborhood attractive to criminal operations that the residents did not invite and cannot easily expel
Biofoam instability — the 'lost in transit' Gravemoss material is sometimes defective batches, and structural failures have killed people
opportunities: Anonymity — Slavic Breaks is one of the few places in the Cleveland sprawl with no surveillance infrastructure, making it valuable to anyone who needs to disappear
Community trust — earning the social clubs' trust opens access to a mutual aid network that spans the city's excluded population
Salvage expertise — the neighborhood's repair and manufacturing capabilities are sought by operators who need equipment maintained off the books
The foreclosure houses contain pre-collapse infrastructure — fiber optic lines, copper wiring, sometimes things more interesting — that nobody has fully mapped
story_hooks: A sealed basement in one of the foreclosure houses has been opened, revealing a pre-collapse data cache that contains financial records someone in the current corponation hierarchy would kill to suppress
Saint Stanislaus' unlicensed augmentation practice has attracted the attention of Tessera's enforcement division — and the neighborhood is preparing to resist
The Gravemoss biofoam supply chain has been disrupted, and without it, a third of the neighborhood's housing stock will begin to fail within months
frequented_by: Excluded residents and Tier 1 workers who call this home
Operators who need equipment repaired or modified without questions or records
Runners moving through unmonitored territory between the west side and the lakefront
Gravemoss supply chain workers who 'lose' shipments with reliable imprecision
